QF.id: AIFM CIII Legal Documents and Negotiations_9

question.text: An anchor LP in Himalaya Arbitrage Fund insists on a 'Most Favoured Nation' (MFN) clause in its side letter. Which of the following BEST describes the MFN clause's purpose?

answer.text: It guarantees the investor a minimum return equal to the highest-performing scheme of the AIF.
It entitles the investor to elect side-letter benefits granted to any other current or future investor, protecting against less-favourable terms.
It gives the investor a right of first refusal on future schemes of the Manager.
It forces the Manager to charge the same fee to ALL investors, eliminating differential treatment.

explanation.text: The Logic: Chapter 9.4.1 footnote 85 defines the MFN clause as allowing an investor to receive side-letter entitlements that can be used to protect themselves from less favourable terms compared to those offered to other current or future investors. MFN is about CHOOSING better terms, not about uniform pricing. The Trap: Option A confuses MFN with a return guarantee (never permitted). Option C confuses with ROFR. Option D (uniform pricing) is the opposite of MFN — MFN PRESERVES differential treatment by letting the holder cherry-pick. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-D Cat I/II covers MFN in LPA context. XIX-B discusses MFN as a negotiation tool from the client side. XXI-B (Portfolio Manager) has no MFN analogue since PMS is a bilateral service contract. Manager's Pro-Tip: Cap the MFN at 'side letters signed within the same commitment class / ticket size' — otherwise a USD 1 million investor could cherry-pick a USD 50 million investor's fee break, creating fiduciary mismatch.
